title: Model Selection and Token Efficiency in Cursor
description:
In this workshop, we covered through how to think about model selection and token efficiency in Cursor.

Key points covered:

Context is your biggest lever:

75% of output quality is set by the model itself. The remaining 25% comes from context. Use the @ symbol to point Cursor directly at relevant files instead of letting the agent search. This shortens the path to a correct answer and reduces wasted tokens.

Plan with a strong model, build with a fast one:

Use a thinking model (Sonnet, GPT-5.4) in Plan Mode to generate a structured, dependency-aware plan before any code is written. Then switch to a cheaper, faster model like Composer 1.5 to execute it. Catching mistakes at the planning stage is far more token-efficient than fixing them mid-implementation.

Sub-agents for parallel, isolated work:

Spin up sub-agents for tasks where only the output matters (e.g., generating architecture docs, running tests). Each sub-agent runs in its own isolated context, keeping your main thread clean. You can run multiple sub-agents in parallel and assign each its own model.

Skills for reusable, auto-invoked workflows:

Create skills in .cursor/skills/ and the agent will invoke them automatically when relevant. Skills can bundle companion scripts and reference files together. Place them in \~/.cursor/skills/ to make them available across all workspaces.

Multi-model comparison for high-stakes tasks:

Run the same task across multiple models simultaneously using Cursor's multiple models mode. Each runs in its own git worktree, and a built-in judge reviews all outputs and recommends the best one: useful for calibrating which model to standardize on. Note: you pay for each model run.

Cache management:

Switching models mid-conversation breaks the cache, as does editing rules or skills during a session. Keep static content stable to maximize cache hits. When a conversation grows long, use /summarize manually with a specific focus area, then carry that summary into a fresh chat - rather than relying on Cursor's automatic summarization, which weights everything equally.

segments.heading: Core Concepts and Architectural Foundations of Model Selection and Token Efficiency in Cursor
segments.text: In this session on Model Selection and Token Efficiency in Cursor, the focus centers on understanding the practical design patterns and developer workflows enabled by modern AI-assisted engineering. As development teams adopt agentic systems, the boundaries between manual code authorship and automated synthesis begin to blur. The speakers emphasize that establishing reliable context is paramount: providing the right repository structure, explicit project rules, and scoped documentation allows the underlying models to generate precise, syntactically correct implementations. By anchoring the discussion in real-world scenarios, the talk demonstrates how engineering productivity accelerates when tools operate directly within the IDE, reducing friction and eliminating disruptive context switching across disjointed external interfaces.

segments.heading: Technical Implementation, Tooling, and Workflow Patterns
segments.text: Diving deeper into operational mechanics, the presentation details how specific platform capabilities interact to execute complex programming tasks. Key components such as Cursor, Cursor CLI, VS Code work in concert to maintain project state and navigate intricate dependency graphs. The session highlights the importance of deterministic tool calling, background agent execution, and structured feedback loops. Developers are guided through concrete demonstrations showing how natural language prompts are parsed into multi-file diffs, verified against local unit tests, and iteratively refined before final commit. This pattern ensures high reliability across both legacy refactoring and greenfield service development.

segments.heading: Evaluation, Best Practices, and Future Directions
segments.text: The concluding segment addresses best practices for scaling agent-driven development across larger teams. Speakers discuss token efficiency, model selection economics, and safety guardrails required when granting agents access to internal APIs and production repositories. Teams must establish clear evaluation benchmarks to verify that automated contributions maintain rigorous security and code quality standards. By combining automated linting, continuous integration checks, and human-in-the-loop review, organizations can safely harness autonomous agents to resolve routine maintenance tasks, documentation updates, and cross-repository migrations while preserving engineering velocity.
